> 人之生也柔弱，其死也堅強.

Chapter 75 named what had been taken. Chapter 76 is about what remains when something has been taken past a certain point: rigidity.

Four characters, all from carpentry and bow-making.

## 柔 is "can bend and can straighten"

柔: 木曲直也 — the wood that can be bent and can be straightened. Duan Yucai's gloss: any wood that can go from bent to straight, and from straight to bent, is 柔.

So 柔 is not "soft." It is reversible.

## 弱 is bent wood

弱: 橈也 — 橈 is curved wood, the top of the character drawn bent.

So 弱 is not "weak." It is the shape a piece of wood takes and can leave.

## 堅 is hard earth

堅: 剛也, from 土. Earth that has set.

## 強 is a bow drawn full

強: 弓有力也, from 弓. A drawn bow — the stored force at full extension.

## Two pairs, two families

柔 and 弱 belong to wood: bendable and bent.
堅 and 強 belong to earth and bow: set and at full draw.

So 柔弱 versus 堅強 is not soft versus hard. It is can-bend versus cannot-bend. It is reversible versus irreversible.

## 折 is an axe cutting grass

折: 斷也, from 斤 (the axe) and 艸 (the grass).

So 木強則折 is a picture, not a proverb: the hard wood is not bent — it is cut. The soft wood is bent, and bent wood comes back. The hard wood is severed, and severed does not rejoin.

## 草木之生也柔脆

脆 is the other side of the same thing: easy to break, and able to send up again. A green shoot breaks and puts out another. A dry one is 枯槁 — and 枯槁 is the state in which nothing more can come.

## 兵強則滅

A strong army is destroyed.

The line is the same claim as chapter 30's 物壯則老, expressed in the bow's language: at full draw, everything is stored tension, and stored tension has no reserve.

## 強大處下，柔弱處上

The hard and the strong go below; the soft and the weak go above.

This is not a moral ranking. It is a statement about position in a system: what can yield sits at the top where it meets the force, and what cannot yield is placed underneath where it takes the load.

Which is chapter 43's argument arriving as an image of a structure.

## Why this follows 75

75: the dike, and the pressure behind it.
76: what the dike is made of. Hard earth sets, and setting is what breaks.

The two chapters describe a single failure: force that cannot bend is force that must break.

## A test

Take one thing about yourself that has set — an opinion, a routine, a way of speaking. Ask whether it can bend and come back, or whether it would have to be cut. The answer is usually visible in how you respond when it is pushed.
